name: Interface Segregation Principle
intent: Give each client an interface that holds only what that client needs, so that implementers are not forced to write methods they cannot honour and clients are not disturbed by changes to methods they never call.
scenario: A device interface offers print, scan and fax. A basic printer and an office machine implement it, and five clients use it: a print dialog, scan-to-email, a fax desk, a copy shortcut and a health monitor. Then a staple method is added, a label printer is introduced, and print gets a new parameter. The team compares one fat interface, role interfaces cut by client need, and one interface per method.
problem: A fat interface couples everything to everything. The basic printer must implement scan and fax even though it can do neither, so it ships methods that throw NotImplemented or silently do nothing, and a caller can only find out at runtime. Every client depends on the whole interface, so adding a method to it, or changing one signature, can mean retesting (and, in statically compiled languages, often recompiling) clients that never call the method. The usual fix is to split the interface, but split by the wrong axis, or too far, and the result is a pile of interfaces that nobody can find or understand.

howItWorks.title: Start from what each client calls
howItWorks.text: List the methods each client really uses. The print dialog calls print and setPaper, scan-to-email calls scan and scanToEmail, and the health monitor calls status and reset. These sets are the demand side. The interface should be shaped by them, not by what one implementation happens to offer.

howItWorks.title: Cut role interfaces by client need
howItWorks.text: Group methods that the same clients use together: Printing, Scanning, Faxing, Admin. A client depends only on the roles it needs, and a device implements the roles it can really do. The basic printer implements Printing and Admin, and has no scan or fax methods to stub.

howItWorks.title: Watch changes stay local
howItWorks.text: When a Finishing role with a staple method is added, no existing client depends on it, so none is affected. With one fat interface, adding staple affects all 5 clients and forces every device, including the basic printer, to add a method. A changed signature for print then affects only the clients of the Printing role.

howItWorks.title: Notice the roles are never perfect
howItWorks.text: A role is a compromise. A label printer that can print and report status but has no paper tray must still implement all of Printing and Admin, so it writes 2 stubs even with role interfaces. That is the signal to split the role again, or to decide that two stubs are an acceptable price for a simpler design.

howItWorks.title: Stop before one method per interface
howItWorks.text: Cutting further, to one interface per method, removes all stubs and all unused methods, but the family now has 9 interfaces and every client that needs two methods depends on two interfaces. Counting interfaces to understand is part of the cost. Split until no client depends on much it does not use, and stop when the next split only adds names: with roles the copy shortcut still sees setPaper and scanToEmail, and removing those 2 would take the per-method extreme.

pros: Implementers write only methods they can really do, with no stubs that throw
Changes to one capability do not disturb clients of the others
Clients are easy to test with a small fake of just the roles they use
Each interface describes a capability that can be named
cons: More interfaces to name, find and keep consistent
A client that needs several capabilities depends on several interfaces
Roles cut by today's clients may need re-cutting when new clients appear
In languages without interfaces, the benefit comes from convention, not from the compiler
whenToUse: An implementation has methods that throw NotImplemented or do nothing
A change to one method forces recompiling or retesting clients that never call it
Clients need very different parts of the same large interface
whenNotToUse: A small interface that every client uses entirely: splitting it adds names for nothing
Before there are clients with different needs: the roles would be guesses
To produce one method per interface everywhere: that is not what the principle asks
pitfalls: Confusing it with one-method interfaces everywhere, which gives dozens of interfaces nobody can find
Splitting by implementer (BasicPrinterDevice, OfficeDevice) instead of by what clients need
Leaving the NotImplemented smell in place and documenting which methods not to call
Roles that are too coarse, so some device still writes stubs for half of a role
Splitting a fat interface into parts, then having every client take all the parts again
Cutting the interfaces by the first implementation, before the clients show what they need

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Code that calls some of the device's methods.

roles.label: Interface
roles.description: The set of methods a client depends on.

roles.label: Basic printer
roles.description: Can print and report status, nothing more.

roles.label: Developer
roles.description: Adds methods and devices over time.

quiz.question: A BasicPrinter implements a Device interface and throws NotImplemented in scan() and fax(). What does this tell you?
options: The interface asks implementers for more than some of them can do, and should be split.
The printer should be changed to scan and fax, to match the interface.
The exceptions are fine as long as the clients catch them everywhere.
The interface is correct and the printer should not implement it at all.
quiz.explanation: Stubs that throw are the typical sign of a fat interface: it promises more than an implementer can deliver, and callers find out at runtime. Splitting it by what clients need lets the printer implement only what it can do.

quiz.question: A team cuts a device interface into IBasicPrinterDevice and IOfficeDevice, one per implementation. Why does this miss the point of the principle?
options: Because interfaces should never be named after devices.
Because two interfaces are always too few to split anything.
Because the split follows the implementers, and clients still depend on methods they never call.
Because office devices cannot implement more than one interface.
quiz.explanation: The principle is about what the client needs. An interface cut by implementer still lists many methods for each client, and a client that only prints depends on the scan and fax methods of the office interface.

quiz.question: A device family has 9 methods and 5 clients. A team makes one interface per method: no stubs, no unused methods. What is the main cost?
options: Clients can no longer be compiled separately from the devices.
Devices must implement more methods than before.
Every change to a signature now affects all clients.
There are 9 interfaces to understand, and clients that need two methods depend on two interfaces.
quiz.explanation: The extreme removes the noise but multiplies the interfaces: more names to find, and more dependencies to declare. Roles cut by client need keep the benefit with fewer interfaces, here 5 instead of 9.
